---

<p class="section-label">How Shiny runs code by default</p>

Shiny is **single-threaded and sequential**. Tasks queue up and run one at a time.

:::{.cr-section}

:::{#cr-sync}
```{=html}
<div class="sticky-card">
  <p style="font-weight:600; margin-bottom: 1.2rem; color:#555;">Synchronous execution for 4 tasks</p>
  <div class="task-row">
    <span class="task-label">Task A</span>
    <div class="task-bar" style="width:80px;"></div>
    <span style="color:#888; font-size:0.85rem;">2s</span>
  </div>
  <div class="task-row">
    <span class="task-label">Task B</span>
    <div class="task-bar waiting" style="width:80px;"></div>
    <div class="task-bar" style="width:160px;"></div>
    <span style="color:#888; font-size:0.85rem;">4s</span>
  </div>
  <div class="task-row">
    <span class="task-label">Task C</span>
    <div class="task-bar waiting" style="width:240px;"></div>
    <div class="task-bar" style="width:200px;"></div>
    <span style="color:#888; font-size:0.85rem;">5s</span>
  </div>
  <div class="task-row">
    <span class="task-label">Task D</span>
    <div class="task-bar waiting" style="width:440px;"></div>
    <div class="task-bar" style="width:120px;"></div>
    <span style="color:#888; font-size:0.85rem;">3s</span>
  </div>
  <div class="total-row">Total: 14 seconds</div>
</div>
```
:::

:::{#cr-async}
```{=html}
<div class="sticky-card">
  <p style="font-weight:600; margin-bottom: 1.2rem; color:#555;">Asynchronous execution for 4 tasks</p>
  <div class="task-row">
    <span class="task-label">Task A</span>
    <div class="task-bar" style="width:80px;"></div>
    <span style="color:#888; font-size:0.85rem;">2s</span>
  </div>
  <div class="task-row">
    <span class="task-label">Task B</span>
    <div class="task-bar" style="width:160px;"></div>
    <span style="color:#888; font-size:0.85rem;">4s</span>
  </div>
  <div class="task-row">
    <span class="task-label">Task C</span>
    <div class="task-bar" style="width:200px;"></div>
    <span style="color:#888; font-size:0.85rem;">5s</span>
  </div>
  <div class="task-row">
    <span class="task-label">Task D</span>
    <div class="task-bar" style="width:120px;"></div>
    <span style="color:#888; font-size:0.85rem;">3s</span>
  </div>
  <div class="total-row" style="color: #2d8a5a;">Total: 5 seconds</div>
</div>
```
:::

A user clicks a button. Shiny starts a slow operation like a database query, an API call, or running a heavy model. @cr-sync

Everything else waits. The user is "frozen". If other users share the same R process, they wait too. @cr-sync

The total runtime is the *sum* of all tasks. That adds up fast. @cr-sync

This is what you want: tasks run at the same time. The total time is the duration of the *longest* task and not the sum of all of them. @cr-async

:::

---

<p class="section-label">Two levels of blocking</p>

Who's waiting? Just the user who triggered the task? Or everyone sharing the R process? Or both?

:::{.cr-section}

:::{#cr-table-sync}
```{=html}
<div class="sticky-card">
  <table class="async-table">
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th>Approach</th>
        <th>Other users unblocked?</th>
        <th>Current user unblocked?</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr>
        <td>Synchronous code</td>
        <td><span class="cross">✗</span></td>
        <td><span class="cross">✗</span></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>Async with promises / futures</td>
        <td><span class="check">✓</span></td>
        <td><span class="partial">~ workaround</span></td>
      </tr>
      <tr class="highlight-row">
        <td><strong>ExtendedTask</strong></td>
        <td><span class="check">✓</span></td>
        <td><span class="check">✓</span></td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</div>
```
:::

**Cross-session** blocking means one user's slow task freezes other users sharing the same R process. Async programming with `promises` (amongst others) already solves this. @cr-table-sync

But the user who *triggered* the task is still completely frozen. They can't interact with the app at all while it runs. That's **inner-session** blocking. Something `promises` *can* do, but wasn't designed to do. @cr-table-sync

**ExtendedTask** solves both. Your session stays alive. The clock keeps ticking. The app stays interactive while the task runs in the background. @cr-table-sync

:::

---

<p class="section-label">What is ExtendedTask?</p>

:::{.cr-section}

:::{#cr-definition}
```{=html}
<div class="sticky-card">
  <p style="font-size:1.5rem; font-weight:700; line-height:1.5; margin-bottom:1.2rem;">ExtendedTask is Shiny's built-in way to run a slow operation in the background without blocking the user's session.</p>
  <ul style="color:#555; line-height:2; font-size:1rem;">
    <li>Available since Shiny 1.8.1</li>
    <li>Works with <code>mirai</code>, <code>futures</code>, and <code>promises</code> as backends</li>
    <li>One invocation at a time: new calls <strong>queue</strong>, they don't drop</li>
    <li>Built-in integration with <code>bslib::input_task_button()</code></li>
  </ul>
</div>
```
:::

You give it an async function. It runs in the background. The session stays responsive. @cr-definition

If you call `invoke()` while a task is already running, the new call **queues**: it doesn't get dropped or throw an error. @cr-definition

:::

---

<p class="section-label">The simplest possible example</p>

:::{.cr-section}

:::{#cr-simple}
```r
my_task <- ExtendedTask$new(function() {
  mirai({ Sys.sleep(3); 42 })
})

observe({
  my_task$invoke()
}) |> bindEvent(input$go)

output$result <- renderText({
  my_task$result()
})
```
:::

Three things. That's the whole pattern. @cr-simple

**Create**: wrap an async function in `ExtendedTask$new()`. The function returns a `mirai` (or a future or a promise). [@cr-simple]{highlight="1-3"}

**Invoke**: call `invoke()` when you want it to run. Pipe an `observe()` into `bindEvent()`. [@cr-simple]{highlight="5-7"}

**Result**: read `result()` in a render function. It waits silently until the task is done, then returns the value. [@cr-simple]{highlight="9-11"}

:::

---

<p class="section-label">The lifecycle</p>

:::{.cr-section}

:::{#cr-states}
```{=html}
<div class="sticky-card">
  <p style="font-weight:600; color:#555; margin-bottom:1.5rem;">Task lifecycle</p>

  <div class="state-flow">
    <span class="state-badge s-initial">initial</span>
    <span class="state-arrow">→</span>
    <span class="state-badge s-running">running</span>
    <span class="state-arrow">→</span>
    <span class="state-badge s-success">success</span>
  </div>
  <div class="state-flow" style="padding-left:204px;">
    <span class="state-arrow">↘</span>
    <span class="state-badge s-error">error</span>
  </div>

  <div style="margin-top:2rem; font-size:0.9rem; color:#555; line-height:2.2;">
    <div><code>task$status()</code>: reactive, returns the current state as a string</div>
    <div><code>task$result()</code>: reactive, returns the result or rethrows on error</div>
  </div>
</div>
```
:::

When you first create an `ExtendedTask`, it starts in the **initial** state: nothing has happened yet. @cr-states

Call `invoke()` and it moves to **running**. The task is executing in the background. @cr-states

When it finishes cleanly: **success**. `result()` returns the value. If something went wrong: **error**. `result()` rethrows it. @cr-states

Use `status()` to drive your UI:update a badge, record how long it took, show a spinner. @cr-states

:::

---

<p class="section-label">The code</p>

Let's look at how this comes together in practice.

:::{.cr-section}

:::{#cr-full-code}
```r
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(mirai)

run_task <- function(symbol, start_date, end_date) {
  Sys.sleep(5)
  # ... fetch stock data ...
  data.frame(Date = dates, Close = prices)
}

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    selectInput("company", "Company", choices = c(...)),
    dateRangeInput("dates", "Date range", ...),
    input_task_button("task", "Get stock data")
  ),
  echarts4rOutput("stock_plot")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  stock_results <- ExtendedTask$new(
    function(...) mirai(run(symbol, start_date, end_date), ...)
  ) |> bind_task_button("task")

  observe({
    stock_results$invoke(
      symbol     = input$company,
      start_date = input$dates[1],
      end_date   = input$dates[2]
    )
  }) |> bindEvent(input$task)

  observe({
    if (stock_results$status() == "success") {
      # record duration, update badge, etc.
    }
  }) |> bindEvent(stock_results$status())

  output$stock_plot <- renderEcharts4r({
    df <- stock_results$result()
    df |> e_charts(Date) |> e_area(Close)
  })

}
```
:::

This app retrieves stock data. We simulate a delay to mimic a real-world scenario. So... In this case, stock data retrieval takes about 5 seconds. Too long! @cr-full-code

`run_task` returns a plain data frame. Later, a chart is built in the main process from the result. [@cr-full-code]{highlight="5-9"}

`input_task_button` automatically disables while the task runs and re-enables when it's done. No manual wiring needed. [@cr-full-code]{highlight="15"}

`ExtendedTask$new()` wraps your async function. In this case we run it directly with `mirai(run())`, but we also could've wrapped the `run_task` function in `mirai({ ... })` or `future_promise({ ... })`. Both work, but `mirai` is best practice (faster startup time, less per-task overhead, more linear scaling, event-driven vs time-polling). `bind_task_button()` connects it to the button. [@cr-full-code]{highlight="23-26"}

`invoke()` starts the task. Reactive values are passed **as arguments** and not read directly inside the function. [@cr-full-code]{highlight="28-33"}

`status()` lets you react to state changes without touching `result()`. [@cr-full-code]{highlight="35-39"}

`result()` is used directly in a render function. It throws silently while running, so the output simply waits. [@cr-full-code]{highlight="41-44"}

:::

---

<p class="section-label">Two "rules" worth remembering</p>

:::{.cr-section}

:::{#cr-rule1}
```{=html}
<div class="rule-card">
  <p class="rule-title">① Don't read reactive values inside the task function</p>
  <p class="rule-body">The function runs in a separate process with no access to the Shiny session. Pass all reactive values as arguments to <code>invoke()</code> instead.</p>
</div>
```
:::

:::{#cr-rule2}
```{=html}
<div class="rule-card">
  <p class="rule-title">② Don't use <code>result()</code> inside <code>observeEvent()</code>, <code>eventReactive()</code>, <code>bindEvent()</code> or <code>isolate()</code></p>
  <p class="rule-body">Using <code>result()</code> in those places will do nothing: invalidation will be ignored. <code>result()</code> is designed for <code>render*</code> functions. Use <code>status()</code> to react to task completion.</p>
</div>
```
:::

The first thing to know: reactive values inside the task function don't work. @cr-rule1

The second: `result()` belongs in render functions.. @cr-rule2

:::
